title: POC weekly quality triage & prompt fidelity review - Emberfield Systems
summary: Weekly POC sync: reviewed this week's scorecard, identified two regression clusters related to prompt templating and a data drift case. Agreed on short-term mitigations (prompt tightening + soft-fallback routing) and to run a 24h KV-cache-enabled benchmark. Security raised a questions about retention for pilot logs; Redwood to share SOC2 docs and retention config options.
action_items: Maya - send updated scoring spreadsheet with per-case annotations by 2027-10-07
Ethan - spin up 24h KV-cache benchmark on Dedicated-sim and share perf logs by 2027-10-08
Carlos - provide example failing prompts + upstream data slice by 2027-10-06
Olivia - list retention and encryption requirements, and confirm minimum SIEM integration needs by 2027-10-09
Samir - run quick sampling job to flag data schema drift and share output by 2027-10-07
next_steps: Redwood to share SOC 2 and audit log examples
Run KV-cache benchmark and compare token cost and P95 latency
Customer to curate 150-case prompt set for regression bisection
Schedule escalation call with engineering if regression persists after prompt fixes
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2027-10-05 | Time: 14:00 UTC | Duration: 55m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Emberfield PM), Carlos Mendes (Emberfield ML Eng), Olivia Park (Emberfield Security), Samir Rao (Emberfield Data Ops)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick agenda: scorecard review, dig into the two regressions we saw this week, and decide immediate mitigations. Ethan and I will take notes.
[00:18] Priya: Thanks, Maya. Quick reminder - execs want a go/no-go signal by end of pilot, so we need to show stability improvements this sprint. Not asking for perfect but reduction in noisy false positives.
[00:34] Ethan: Understood. We looked at the heatmap you sent; two clusters — one prompt-format sensitivity, and one data-schema drift where newline tokenization threw off intent extraction.
[00:51] Carlos: Yeah that newline thing bit us. A batch from our ingestion pipeline had CR LF vs LF, and the prompt builder concatenated without normalization. So model saw weird tokens.
[01:07] Maya: Okay, so that's partially upstream. For the prompt fidelity cluster — we saw that slight paraphrases cause score downgrades. We want to test tightening templates and fallback policies.
[01:25] Priya: Can you explain fallback policies again? Last time there was some confusion about dedicated vs hosted fallback behavior.
[01:33] Ethan: Sure. Briefly: we have routing policies in the platform — e.g., primary model is the tuned variant, fallback is a slightly larger but more robust variant, or a cached response if prefix matches. For Dedicated we can pin model versions and use a soft-fallback to a variant in the same pool. For hosted we default to the catalog fallback.
[01:55] Olivia: From security — any fallback that logs the full prompt outside our VPC is not acceptable. We need assurance about where fallback execution occurs and log retention.
[02:07] Maya: Good callout. We'll include retention options and show the Private deployment flow for fallbacks — you can keep logs inside your VPC and route fallbacks to on-prem variant. We'll share SOC2 and KMS docs after the call.
[02:25] Samir: Quick Q on KV cache: if we enable prefix KV caching will that affect scoring? We saw slight consistency differences in the cached runs.
[02:36] Ethan: Yes, cache can change early tokens because it preserves previous hidden states; that can alter top-k in long-context prompts. We should benchmark with and without KV caching and check scores as well as latency/cost tradeoffs.
[02:52] Priya: Sounds like a plan. For the two regression clusters, what's your recommended triage order?
[03:00] Ethan: 1) Data normalization fix (CRLF) upstream — Samir's team. 2) Prompt template tightening — reduce optional clauses and add explicit examples. 3) Run KV-cache benchmark to measure differences.
[03:18] Carlos: For prompt tightening, I'll produce a 150-case set highlighting paraphrase failures. Some of the failures are low-confidence model hallucinations when a numeric field is missing.
[03:31] Maya: Good. Please include the exact input and model output. Those help us run bisection.
[03:40] Priya: On scoring — the current threshold was set aggressively to avoid slips. Could we add a soft threshold band to mark items for human review rather than automatic rejection?
[03:51] Ethan: Yes, Redwood supports a triage band. You can mark outputs between 0.45-0.6 as "review" and route them to a human queue. That reduces production churn.
[04:05] Olivia: That raises throughput questions. If too many go to human review, our ops will be overwhelmed. We need expected rates.
[04:13] Maya: We'll estimate expected review load from the score distribution and send a projection with the updated scoring sheet.
[04:21] Priya: Excellent.
[04:30] [05:00] Ethan: Diving into the scorecard — I pulled the weekly snapshot. Overall pass rate fell from 92% to 87%. The two clusters account for ~60% of the drop.
[05:15] Priya: Which cluster is more urgent?
[05:20] Ethan: Prompt fidelity cluster is higher P99 severity for end-user visible errors. Data drift is intermittent but easier to patch.
[05:30] Carlos: Patch for data drift should be quick — normalize newlines and schema checks. I'm aiming to push a fix to staging tonight.
[05:41] Maya: Great. For prompt fixes, can you share one canonical failing example now?
[05:47] Carlos: Sure — input: "Invoice 347 - missing total" output: model inferred currency incorrectly because earlier context included another invoice with a different currency; prompt didn't anchor the currency field. Model answered USD when it should have been EUR.
[06:05] Priya: That was the same one that hit the finance flows, yeah.
[06:10] Ethan: Two mitigation options: 1) anchor prompts with explicit field labels and examples, 2) enforce a pre-parser that extracts currency and injects as a variable. First is faster.
[06:22] Maya: We'll prototype tightened templates today and run them against the 150-case set. If that reduces false positives by >50% we consider it a win.
[06:35] Olivia: Can you also show how guardrails detect hallucinations? We had a false positive case flagged as hallucination but it was actually a correct extrapolation. The rule was too aggressive.
[06:47] Ethan: Our guardrails use lexical checks plus model confidence heuristics. We can tune thresholds and add whitelist rules — e.g., allow numeric extrapolation if supported by precedents in doc. We can also instrument a "why flagged" trace for each case to help tuning.
[07:05] Priya: Is that trace accessible in the console?
[07:09] Maya: Yes, per-request traces show which guardrail fired and why, plus raw token deltas. We'll demo in the next session.
[07:18] [10:00] Priya: Anything on cost? Execs asked whether enabling KV cache reduces cost but increases unpredictability.
[07:27] Ethan: Cache usually reduces per-token compute by ~20-35% for repeat prefixes. But it can make worst-case latency worse for cold-starts. We'll quantify with the benchmark.
[07:38] Maya: We'll include token cost impact in the KV benchmark report.
[07:42] Carlos: On the benchmark — do you need a representative workload? I can export a 24h sample.
[07:48] Ethan: Please do that. We'll replay it on a Dedicated-sim and the hosted variant with caching toggled.
[07:56] Samir: Quick note: our compliance requires logs retention for 180 days and encryption with our KMS. How does Redwood handle per-tenant retention?
[08:06] Maya: For Private deployment we support tenant-controlled retention; for Hosted you can set retention policy and legal hold, but logs are encrypted with Redwood-managed keys by default — we can enable KMS integration (bring-your-own-key) for enterprise. We'll send the SOC2 + KMS integration docs.
[08:24] Olivia: We'll need an explicit SLA about log deletion on contract end.
[08:29] Maya: Noted, we'll include that language in the appendix of the security packet.
[08:35] [15:00] Ethan: Back to regressions — I suggest we run a quick bisection: take the 150-case prompt set, run baseline, then iteratively apply prompt-tightening patches until we isolate the minimal change that reduces failures. We can share a spreadsheet with per-case diffs.
[08:54] Carlos: That approach works. For the bisection, can Redwood run the jobs or do we need to provide infra?
[09:00] Ethan: Redwood can run the bisection on the pilot Dedicated-sim; we'll log outputs and attach deltas to the spreadsheet. That will cost a modest number of tokens — we'll estimate.
[09:12] Priya: Estimate needed for execs.
[09:15] Maya: We'll include the token estimate and projected human review load in the follow-up.
[09:20] Priya: On fallback — if a prompt fails post-triage what behavior do you recommend? Auto-fail, human review, or fallback to conservative variant?
[09:28] Ethan: Conservative variant fallback plus incrementing review score. Route to human queue if below hard-threshold. Also an automatic ticket to the data team if it's high-severity.
[09:37] Olivia: Make sure fallback paths don't exfiltrate PII outside our VPC.
[09:41] Maya: We'll mark that as a hard requirement.
[09:45] [20:00] Samir: Carlos pushed the schema check patch to staging already — quick test earlier showed improvement on a small sample.
[09:54] Carlos: Yes, the CRLF normalization fix reduced the drift cluster by ~40% on our internal test. Full rollout pending a green run.
[10:03] Priya: Nice. Timeline for production?
[10:06] Carlos: If no issues, early next week.
[10:10] Maya: Great. For prompt tightening, what's your ETA, Carlos?
[10:15] Carlos: I can curate the 150-case set today and start the first pass of template changes tomorrow.
[10:21] Ethan: We'll run the bisection Wednesday and return results Thursday.
[10:26] Priya: Perfect.
[10:30] [30:00] Olivia: Security follow-up — besides SOC2 and KMS, we need: SSO via SAML, RBAC for routes, per-route audit logs, and the ability to redact PII before logs are persisted. Can you confirm those exist?
[10:43] Maya: Yes to SAML SSO and RBAC. Per-route audit logs are available; redaction can be configured via the ingestion pipeline. We'll include a config example.
[10:52] Olivia: Also, can we do a one-hour architecture review with your security engineer?
[10:56] Maya: Absolutely — I'll coordinate a separate session.
[10:59] [40:00] Ethan: Small gotcha we noticed — when caching is enabled, the per-request trace shows KV hits but doesn't always include the original prompt snippet due to truncation. We'll surface that in the trace UX so you can see why a cached response matched.
[11:12] Priya: That would help debugging.
[11:15] Maya: We'll prioritize that as a UX tweak.
[11:20] Carlos: For the bisection spreadsheet, please include columns: input, baseline output, tightened-output, score-delta, guardrail-fires, notes.
[11:29] Ethan: Will do.
[11:33] [50:00] Priya: Any blockers?
[11:36] Carlos: No blockers from our side beyond needing the per-case token cost estimates.
[11:40] Olivia: Our blocker is clarifying the log retention and KMS flow; otherwise green.
[11:45] Maya: Action items summarized in the chat and I'll email the scoring sheet and SOC2 packet within 24 hours.
[11:53] Priya: Thank you, team. Looking forward to the KV cache benchmark results.
[11:58] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll reconvene same time next week unless something urgent comes up.
[12:05] End of meeting.
